subject: Trump announces diesel fuel deal with Russia to address elevated prices
posts:
Trump cuts backroom diesel deal with Moscow to soothe midterm voters.
Evidence: Sanction relief for Putin, high domestic pump prices, geopolitical fallout
#Aletheia #USPol #Energy

Trump announced an agreement with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, framing it as necessary relief to lower soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterms.
Stated Judgement: (+0.5, 0.0) — Good Preference

Lifting sanctions to buy Russian diesel funnels cash to Moscow's war machine while undercutting international alliances for short-term domestic political gain.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.8, -0.9) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. A transactional political maneuver trades long-term geopolitical stability for fleeting domestic convenience.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 4)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- White House Messaging: FAIL (-0.8, -0.9) — Frames geopolitical surrender as economic relief.
- Strategic Sanctions: FAIL (-0.9, -0.9) — Undermines Western deterrence.
Facing voter anger over elevated fuel prices during wartime, the administration bypassed sanctions to secure Russian diesel supplies right before midterms.

The Poison:
Trading sanctions enforcement for temporary price relief signals weakness to adversaries and demoralizes allies facing active aggression.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHO is profiting: ordinary citizens absorb geopolitical fallout while the Kremlin secures economic lifelines and leaders buy votes.

Social Physics Analysis:
Actors run a Smart Selfish Maneuver. They manufacture an urgent domestic crisis, deploy a self-serving pretext, and project blame outward while quietly enriching an adversary.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated economic relief and geopolitical surrender, it plots directly toward Greater Evil. F_net collapses under strategic load.

The Unavoidable Truth: Short-term political survival often overrides long-term national security.

The Unavoidable Lie: Appeasing hostile regimes stabilizes domestic energy markets.

Alethekanon:
Convenient backroom deals with aggressors substitute for genuine energy resilience, trading collective security for ephemeral ballot-box optics.

Awwthekanon:
It's heartbreaking to watch political expediency override human solidarity, leaving ordinary people to pay the ultimate price for leaders' compromises.

Brothekanon:
Wild how trading fuel with Moscow gets spun as a domestic win while completely ignoring the obvious security fallout. Politics makes strange bedfellows.

Spirithekanon:
"Woe to those who call evil good and good evil." Isaiah 5:20 FAIL
Trading security for temporary convenience invites greater ruin.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a deal to supply the United States with Russian diesel fuel.

Diesel prices remain a significant issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections amid the war in Iran. Trump administration officials were previously working on freeing up Russian diesel, which had been blocked from being imported into the U.S., as a means of lowering the price of fuel used in the agriculture and transportation sectors.

Kash Patel announces arrest of suspected ShinyHunters co-conspirator after FBI jobs portal breach

FBI Director Kash Patel says agents arrested a suspected ShinyHunters co-conspirator tied to the FBIjobs.gov data breach and third-party vendor hack.

Actual Article Body:

Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory special agent turned CEO of Media Rep Global Strategies, explains how stolen personal and assignment information could be exploited while stressing there is no evidence hackers accessed classified FBI systems.

FBI Director Kash Patel announced Friday that agents arrested another suspected co-conspirator linked to the ShinyHunters hacking group earlier this week, as the bureau investigates a cybersecurity incident involving its jobs website.

The arrest is the latest in a series of FBI actions against the hacking network in recent days, according to Patel, who said investigators are pursuing additional leads and evidence.

"Earlier this week, our agents in the field arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor," Patel said in an Oct. 9 statement.

FBI INVESTIGATES AFTER SHINYHUNTERS HACKERS CLAIM THEFT OF AGENTS' PERSONAL DATA

FBI Director Kash Patel speaks during a press conference on October 23, 2025 in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Patel said the FBI is working with its partners to dismantle the group and its associates.

"This arrest demonstrates the strength and reach of our efforts to protect Americans from cybercrime. We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate."

ShinyHunters, a criminal hacking and extortion group, previously said it obtained sensitive personal information belonging to FBI employees and applicants through the bureau's jobs portal.16-YEAR-OLD ALLEGEDLY LED RANSOMWARE GANG BEHIND HUNDREDS OF ATTACKS

The group said it stole information belonging to nearly all FBI agents and people who applied to work for the bureau, Reuters previously reported. A sample of data shared with the outlet contained agents' names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, assignments and, in some cases, names of family members.

The FBI previously said it was investigating whether the breach originated within its own systems or through a third-party provider supporting FBIJobs.gov. The extent of the alleged breach has not been independently confirmed.

Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and CEO of Media Rep Global Strategies, previously told Fox News Digital that the distinction between stolen personnel information and access to classified investigative systems is critical.

FBI HACK CLAIM RAISES FEARS OVER SENSITIVE PERSONAL DATA

FBI investigators monitor digital threats as questions remain over how the FBIJobs.gov incident occurred and what information may have been exposed. (FBI)

"There is a meaningful difference between somebody obtaining personnel information and somebody gaining access to classified investigative systems," Pack said. "Based on what we know right now, there is no indication they have the keys to the kingdom."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A representative for the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.
